facts.text: About 5,000 years ago, the Sumerians, among the first people known to brew beer, drank it through long, thin tubes.
The tubes let Sumerian drinkers reach the liquid under the solid by-products floating on their beer.
Ancient straws of this kind have been dug up in present-day Iraq, where the Sumerians lived.
Until the late 1800s most people used natural hollow stems such as rye grass or reeds; these broke easily or gave drinks an earthy taste.
Marvin Stone ran a factory in Washington, D.C., that made paper cigarette holders.
In the 1880s Stone wound paper strips around a pencil, glued them and coated the tube with paraffin wax.
Stone patented his paper drinking straw in 1888.
In the decade after the patent, Stone's paper straws became common at soda fountains.
In the 1930s inventor Joseph Friedman made a bendable paper straw after watching his young daughter struggle with a straight one.
Hospitals were among the first to use bendable straws, because patients could drink while lying in bed.
Plastic production grew during and after World War II, and plastic straws appeared in the 1950s.
Plastic straws were cheaper and sturdier than paper ones and over time replaced them.
A 2018 study estimated that up to 8.3 billion plastic straws pollute beaches around the world.
Seattle's ban on plastic straws took effect on 1 July 2018.

From 1 July 2019, about 8,000 places in Taiwan, including government offices, schools, department stores, shopping malls and fast-food chains, stopped giving single-use plastic straws to dine-in customers.
